textTitles: The bridges we stop looking at

texts.title: The bridges we stop looking at

paragraphs.text: A bridge is the rarest kind of public asset: one that almost everybody uses and almost nobody notices. It has no opening hours, no staff at the door and no annual report, and its condition becomes a public subject only when it is closed. That invisibility is not a minor detail of bridge politics; it is the whole of it, because the money that keeps a structure standing has to be argued for against things that voters can see.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Most of the bridges in wealthy countries were built in two bursts, and both are now inconveniently old. The first came with the railways of the nineteenth century, the second with the road building of the decades after 1950, and the second burst was enormous: in several countries more than half of the road bridges in use were completed between 1955 and 1980. Structures built in the same decade tend to need major work in the same decade, which turns an engineering problem into a budgeting one.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Deterioration is mostly chemistry. Concrete protects the steel inside it because it is alkaline, and that protection fails when chlorides reach the bars, whether from sea air or from the salt spread on roads each winter. Once corrosion begins, the rust occupies more space than the metal it replaces, the concrete cracks from within, and water reaches more steel. The process is slow, invisible from a car, and accelerating: the cost of repair roughly doubles for every decade the work is put off.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Inspection has therefore become a discipline of its own. A visual check from a ladder finds what can be seen; the state of the reinforcement is measured by other means, from mapping the electrical potential of the surface to acoustic sensors listening for the sharp sound a steel wire makes when it snaps inside a cable. Several agencies now instrument their largest structures permanently, and the data has produced an uncomfortable finding: the bridges that fail inspection are not always the old ones, and the ones with the worst chemistry are often thirty years old rather than eighty.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Money is allocated in a way that makes deferral rational for everyone involved. Maintenance budgets are annual, political terms are short, and a bridge that is patched will survive another term while a bridge that is properly rebuilt consumes a decade of the budget and produces a photograph of a closed road. Several audits of national programmes have found the same pattern: the work done is the work that is cheap this year, and the backlog grows at a rate that is reported in the appendices rather than in the summary.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Closure is not the only failure, and the commonest one is invisible from outside. A structure judged unsafe for heavy vehicles is rarely demolished; it is posted with a weight limit, and the lorries take a longer route. The cost of that detour, paid in fuel and time by people who never learn why the road is longer, frequently exceeds the cost of the repair that was not done, and it does not appear in any transport budget because it is not paid by the transport department.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The engineering has improved in ways that make the next century easier. Stainless or coated reinforcement, denser concrete mixes, sealed joints that stop water reaching the supports, and drainage designed to be cleaned rather than to be ignored all extend the life of a new structure substantially. None of this helps the existing stock, which is the part that matters now: the bridges that will need attention in the next twenty years are already built, and they were built to the standards of their own decade.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What changes behaviour, where anything does, is publication. Where inspection results are published for each structure, in a form that names the road rather than a reference number, maintenance budgets rise and the backlog stops growing; where results are held internally, they do not. That is a duller conclusion than the engineering deserves, and it fits the pattern of the whole subject: the hard part is not knowing what a bridge needs, but arranging for somebody to be answerable for not doing it. A list nobody reads protects nobody; a list with a road name in it is read by the people who drive along that road every morning.
paragraphs.label: H
